newsitem.title: USA: CBOT to upgrade Project A trading system - Arbo.
newsitem.headline: CBOT to upgrade Project A trading system - Arbo.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) aims to enhance its fast growing Project A electronic after-hours trading system this year mainly through improving accessibility, CBOT chairman Patrick Arbor said.
"To ensure continued viability of Project A, we are upgrading its technology," Arbor said at the exchange's annual meeting on Thursday.

Plans include the implementation of interface to give traders dial-in access through their own personal computers, and the launching of conventional Project A work-stations in London and elsewhere in Europe, Arbor said.

He said development was under way for a common switch that would let traders use a single terminal for both Project A and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange's (CME) GLOBEX, an electronic trading system developed by CME, France's Matif SA and Reuters Holdings Plc.
Project A had a record volume of 2,438,712 contracts in 1996, up 358 percent from 531,928 a year earlier, CBOT senior vice president Glen Johnson said.
With that turnover, the Project A division of Ceres Trading Limited Partnership, which operates the system, had a profit of $2,373,442 in 1996 against a loss of $1,389,363 in 1995, he reported.
Arbor said Ceres should be able to distribute $1 million to CBOT membership this year if volume stays at the same level and expenses within budget.

"While this is not necessarily a lot of money in the big scheme of things -- it's a little less than $500 per member -- it does represent a significant first time development," he said. He called 1996 a "breakthrough year" for Project A.
Arbor said Project A volume was averaging more than 17,000 contracts a day so far in 1997 against 9,700 in 1996.
For the PC interface, 10 to 20 members will begin a two-month "beta test" on May 1, moving into the "production stage" on July 1, Arbor said.
For the conventional Project A terminals, one work station will begin operation in London on July 1 and other European cities would follow "based on demand," he added.
There are currently 165 Project A terminals -- 85 at CBOT, 62 in the Chicago area, 17 in New York and one in Memphis.
Asked if CBOT planned to join CME in adopting the French NSC electronic trading system and use CME's Clearing 21 trade processing system, Arbor flatly said, "No."

Common clearing for all U.S. futures exchanges is a goal and the CBOT/CME joint strategic initiative committee is looking into merging the Chicago exchanges' back-office functions, but there is no plan to join NSC/Clearing 21 group, he said.

CME and the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) earlier this month said they had signed a letter of intent to adopt the NSC system developed by SBF-Paris Bourse and Matif, and that the NSC users would use Clearing 21, developed by CME and NYMEX.
